sentences.text: Researchers followed 1,370 community-dwelling people aged at least 65 for four years to measure the blood protein Tsukushi at the study's start, providing the first forward-looking clinical proof that its levels connect to sarcopenia development.

Participants with lower initial Tsukushi amounts were more likely to develop sarcopenia later, a link that was stronger for women than men, after statistical tools tested whether the relationship followed a straight line or a curve.

Using Tsukushi levels alone predicted future muscle loss with moderate accuracy, but adding other clinical factors improved the prediction score, leading authors to conclude that the protein is a useful marker when combined with standard data.
